computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: Fe–10Mn–10Al–0.7C composition; equilibrium phase fractions (α, γ, κ, L) computed for temperatures over 550 °C
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: General trend of phase fractions similar to XRD-measured values; the calculated κ-carbide solvus (823 °C) is lower than the measured κ-carbide dissolution temperature (between 850 °C and 900 °C for 1 h annealing), attributed to the non-equilibrium state of the steel and to atomic vs. volume fraction bases.

interfaces.interface_notes: When the annealing temperature rises to 850 °C, κ-carbide in the γ phase area has disappeared, and κ-carbide near the γ phase area has significantly reduced; κ-carbide dispersed continuously along α/α boundaries still exists without much change.
interfaces.phase_evolution: With the increase of annealing temperature, the κ-carbide distributed at or near the boundary of α phase and γ phase dissolves first and the κ-carbide along α/α boundaries of large grains dissolves last; the dissolution temperature of κ-carbide along α/α boundary is higher than that along α/γ boundary in the present steel.

phase_interfaces.coherence: κ-carbide dispersed continuously along α/α boundaries; dissolution temperature along α/α boundary higher than along α/γ boundary

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: A 20 kg ingot of a Fe–10Mn–10Al–0.7C steel was prepared by vacuum induction melting method.
The ingot was heated to 1200 °C and then forged to forging blank with cross section of about 40 mm × 60 mm.
After homogenized at 1200 °C for 1 h, the forging blank was hot-rolled.
The forging blank was hot-rolled to the plate of 3 mm thickness, with the finishing rolling temperature around 880 °C.
After hot rolling the plate was water quenched to about 300 °C.
The hot-rolled plate was annealed at 850 °C (within the range 700–1200 °C) for 1 h.
Annealing was followed by water quenching.

structures.overall_structure: Annealed 850 °C specimen consists of ferrite (α), austenite (γ) and κ-carbide (κ); banded structure and long strip α phase remain after annealing. κ-carbide in the γ phase area has disappeared and κ-carbide near the γ phase area has significantly reduced, while κ-carbide dispersed continuously along α/α boundaries still exists without much change.

unmapped_findings: Product of strength and ductility of the 850 °C annealed specimen is 19 GPa% (Table 1).
Lattice parameters from XRD of the annealed specimens: α phase 2.89–2.91 Å, γ phase 3.65–3.67 Å, κ-carbide 3.76–3.79 Å (b0027).

The N–W (Nishiyama–Wasserman) orientation relationship between κ-carbide and α matrix is found mainly between lamellar κ-carbide and α at 700 °C and is hardly found once the annealing temperature reaches 800 °C (and 850 °C) (b0047).

For the 850 °C specimen the work hardening rate is higher in the early stage (true strain < about 5%), being in the reverse order of the annealing temperatures, and decreases quickly to become lower than the 900 °C specimen in the later stage (b0035, b0063).
The actual dissolution temperature for κ-carbide with 1 h annealing is between 850 °C and 900 °C, higher than the Thermo-Calc value of about 823 °C (b0052, b0033).

In the Fe–Mn–Al–C steel comparison (Table 2), the present steel (855 MPa ultimate / 651 MPa yield / γ + α(40%) + boundary κ / 36.6% elongation / 31 GPa%) has the lowest ultimate elongation and lowest strength–ductility product of the set, attributed to the highest α phase fraction, boundary κ-carbide and inhomogeneous microstructure (b0071, table_002).
No obvious TRIP or TWIP phenomenon was found during the tensile test according to TEM examination of the deformed microstructure (b0040).

No obvious superlattice spots were seen in the SADPs of α or γ phase in the annealed specimens; ordering of atoms in α or γ is not expected during annealing at 700–1200 °C for 1 h, though ordering may occur during quenching (b0033).
